Al Jazeera — published 26 Sep 2026 (approx 14:50 BST; search index showed "2 hours ago" at 16:50 BST)

HEADLINE: Is Ethiopia on the verge of another civil war as fighting erupts in Tigray?

Intensified fighting between Ethiopia's federal army and forces from the northern region of Tigray has raised fears that the peace agreement that ended a devastating two-year war in 2022 could collapse.

FACTS:
- Fighting locations: southern Tigray, spreading into the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions. Overnight fighting in the border town of Abala in northern Afar (Tigray-Afar border).
- Ethiopia's army CLAIMS it "killed more than 270 rebel fighters" — UNVERIFIED claim by the army.
- Ground troop offensives and drone strikes reported.
- Tigrayan forces seized the airports at Mekelle, Axum and Shire, disrupting civilian flights.
- About three-quarters of a million people remained displaced within Tigray BEFORE this escalation.
- The government accuses Eritrea of backing the new alliance; Eritrea has repeatedly denied supporting the armed groups. Relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara deteriorated partly over Abiy Ahmed's push for access to Red Sea ports.
- During the 2020-2022 war, federal troops, Eritrean forces and some fighters from neighbouring Amhara fought against Tigrayan forces. That conflict killed hundreds of thousands, displaced millions and left Tigray largely cut off.
- Fighters from Amhara, who fought alongside the federal army in 2020-2022, took control of western Tigray. Hundreds of thousands of Tigrayans were driven from their homes; Tigrayan leaders now want the territory returned and the displaced allowed home. Many in Amhara reject Tigray's claim, arguing western Tigray should not have been incorporated into Tigray when Ethiopia's regional boundaries were redrawn in 1992.
- The TPLF faction led by Debretsion Gebremichael retook control of Tigray's administration earlier this year, displacing an interim administration established under the peace agreement.
- Tigrayan and Amhara members of the new alliance still have competing claims to western Tigray.

QUOTES:
- Jervin Naidoo, senior political analyst at Oxford Economics Africa: "Since the end of the war, while the Pretoria Agreement has held, there have been consistent violations on both sides."
- Catherine Soi, Al Jazeera correspondent: "There has been overnight fighting in the border town of Abala."

CROSS-REFERENCE (BBC, approved, published ~00:50 BST 26 Sep — 16h before 16:50 BST):
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6d94wywx0ypo
"Are Ethiopians marching back to war in Tigray?" — BBC Africa. Fighting has erupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray between regional forces and the national army. The African Union (AU) brokered the peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, ending the war nearly four years ago, but several unresolved issues have inflamed tensions. The government has accused Eritrea of supporting armed groups inside Ethiopia, something Asmara denies. During the recent civil war Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian troops but the two neighbours have again fallen out. Ethiopia, the world's most populous landlocked nation, lost access to ports when Eritrea seceded in 1993. Recently PM Abiy has been pushing for ownership of Eritrea's southern port of Assab — about 60km (37 miles) from the border — and hinted at taking it by force. There is a fear that Eritrea could be drawn in again, this time against the government.
